title: User information: who, where, when?
lead: Use whoami, id, who, w, last, lastb and getent to see who exists on the system, who is logged in, and where accounts are stored.
objectives: You read your own identity (UID, GID, groups) with `whoami`, `id` and `groups`.
You know what `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/group` and `/etc/shadow` hold and what their fields mean.
You see who is connected now with `who` and `w`, successful logins with `last` and failed ones with `lastb`.
You query accounts with `getent`, no matter whether they live in a file or a central directory (LDAP/SSSD).

sections.title: Who am I? whoami, id, groups
body: Linux is a multi-user system. Every process runs as some user and permissions depend on it. To understand why a command fails, first find out **who you are** and which groups you belong to.

The `id` output looks like `uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=...`. The UID is the numeric identity of the user; the kernel works with **numbers**, not names. `root` is always UID 0. Usually UIDs from 1000 up belong to human users and lower ones to system accounts.

commands.where: To confirm who you are after sudo or su.
commands.why: Prevents working as the wrong user.

commands.what: Shows UID, primary GID and all groups.
commands.where: For permission problems and checking new accounts.
commands.why: Shows which groups give a user access.

commands.what: Lists the names of the groups you belong to.
commands.why: Gives a more readable summary than id.

sections.tip: `id username` also works for other users; if the account does not exist you get `no such user`. It is the quickest way to test whether an account exists.

sections.title: Account files: passwd, group, shadow
body: Local accounts live in three plain-text files. **/etc/passwd** is world-readable; each line has 7 colon-separated fields: `name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell`. The `x` means the password is not stored here.

Password hashes are in **/etc/shadow**, readable only by root. **/etc/group** holds group name, GID and members. The `/sbin/nologin` shell means the account cannot log in interactively (a service account).

`getent` queries the same information from all configured sources (files, LDAP, SSSD). In corporate environments users may not be in `/etc/passwd` at all, so scripts should prefer `getent passwd` over `cat /etc/passwd`.

commands.where: When you need home directory and shell information.

commands.what: Extracts field 1 (user name) from colon-separated data.
commands.why: Pulls the column you need from large files.

commands.what: Finds the line of one specific user.
commands.where: When checking a single account record.
commands.why: Faster than reading the whole list.

commands.what: Looks the account up in all sources (file, LDAP, SSSD).
commands.where: On corporate servers and in scripts.
commands.why: Also finds users from the central directory.

commands.what: Queries a group and its members.
commands.where: To check who is in which group.

sections.tip: `cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd` shows user name and shell side by side; entries with `nologin` are service accounts.
sections.warn: Do not edit `/etc/passwd` or `/etc/shadow` by hand in a text editor. One wrong character can break everyone's login. Manage accounts with tools like `useradd` and `usermod` (module 4.2).

sections.title: Who is connected now? who and w
body: Before maintenance, a reboot or stopping a service, check whether someone else is working on the server. `who` shows connected users, their terminal (`tty1`, `pts/0`) and login time; for remote logins the IP appears in parentheses.
`w` is more detailed: the first line shows uptime and the **load average**, then for each session the idle time (IDLE) and the command being run (WHAT).

commands.what: Shows logged-in users, terminals and times.
commands.why: You will not interrupt someone's work by accident.

commands.what: Shows sessions, idle time, running command and load average.
commands.where: When the server is slow or you look for suspicious sessions.
commands.why: Answers who is doing what in one command.

sections.tip: If only one session is open on your VM, only you appear. Open a second terminal tab and run `who` again; the count goes up.

sections.title: Login history: last and lastb
body: `last` reads `/var/log/wtmp` and lists **successful** logins, logouts and reboots (`reboot`). A common mistake: searching `last` for failed attempts. Failed logins do not appear in `last`.

Failed login attempts are stored in `/var/log/btmp` and read with `lastb`; only root can read it. If you suspect brute-forcing, run `sudo lastb | head` first. On some distributions the btmp file may not exist and the command errors; that can simply mean no failed attempts were ever recorded.

commands.what: Lists successful logins/logouts and reboot records.
commands.where: When investigating who logged in at night.

sections.tip: `last -n 5 student` shows only the last 5 logins of the `student` account.
sections.warn: Login records are sensitive (user names, IP addresses). Remove IPs and names before sharing output on public forums.

t01.text: Find out which user you are running as with `whoami`.

t02.text: Show your UID, GID and group list with `id`.

t03.text: Print your groups with the `groups` command.

t04.text: Look at another user's identity with `id alice`.
t04.hint: Pass the user name as the argument.

t05.hint: The file is readable by everyone.

t06.text: Find only the line of the `student` account with `grep student /etc/passwd`.
t06.hint: Field 6 of the line is the home directory.

t07.text: List only the user names with `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd`.
t07.hint: -d sets the delimiter, -f the field number.

t08.text: Count how many accounts exist with `wc -l /etc/passwd`.
t08.hint: -l counts lines; each line is one account.

t09.text: Predict: how many lines (groups) does `/etc/group` have? Guess first, then verify with `wc -l /etc/group`.
t09.hint: Count the groups root, wheel, student, alice, devs.

t10.text: Predict: what does `cat /etc/shadow` do as a normal user? Think first, then run it.
t10.hint: Password hashes are root-only: Permission denied|Erişim engellendi|Zugriff verweigert.

t11.text: Predict: what does `id bob` return for a user that does not exist? Run it and read the error.
t11.hint: Expect a `no such user` error; the exit code is not 0.

t12.text: Debug: a ticket says `alice` cannot log in. In `~/Documents/accounts.txt` find alice's line and write her shell (field 7) into `~/alice_shell.txt`.
t12.hint: `grep alice FILE | cut -d: -f7 > TARGET`. A `nologin` shell blocks interactive login.

t13.text: Mini project: write the names of accounts whose shell ends in `/bin/bash` in `/etc/passwd` into `~/shell_users.txt`.

t14.text: Challenge: put your user name (`whoami`) and then the `id` output into `~/me.txt`. It must show `student`, `uid=1000` and `wheel`.
t14.hint: Use `>` for the first command and `>>` for the second.

t15.text: Challenge: how many accounts in `/etc/passwd` have the `nologin` shell? Write the number into `~/nologin_count.txt`.
t15.hint: `grep -c` counts matching lines; redirect the output with `>`.

t16.text: TICKET #4107: The auditor wants the UID and groups of `alice`. Save the information in `~/alice_info.txt`.
t16.hint: `id alice > ~/alice_info.txt`; the output must contain `uid=1001` and `devs`.

vm.intro: These commands only read, so you can run them safely on your VM. `lastb` needs `sudo`. Remove IPs and user names before sharing output.

v01.title: Who is connected?

blocks.expected:
student  pts/0   2026-11-12 09:00 (192.168.1.10)
 09:20:01 up 1 day,  2:30,  1 user,  load average: 0.00, 0.01, 0.05
USER     TTY      FROM      LOGIN@   IDLE   WHAT
...

differs: If there are no lines you may be in a graphical session's fake terminal; try a real terminal.
On WSL `who` may be empty; the load average line of `w` is enough.

v02.title: Successful logins
v02.text: List the latest logins and paste the output.

blocks.expected:
student  pts/0  192.168.1.10  Wed Nov 12 09:00   still logged in
reboot   system boot  5.14.0  Wed Nov 12 08:55 still running

wtmp begins Mon Nov 10 08:00:00 2026

differs: If you see `command not found`: `sudo apt install util-linux` (Ubuntu) or `sudo dnf install util-linux` (Rocky/Alma).
In containers or WSL wtmp may be empty; the final `wtmp begins` line is enough.

v03.title: Failed logins
v03.text: Look at the `lastb` output. The list may be empty; that is normal. Then press "Done".
differs: `No such file or directory` (no btmp): no failed login was ever recorded.
You can generate an entry by entering a wrong password in a second terminal (e.g. `su - alice`) and looking again.

v04.title: Query an account with getent
v04.text: Get the record of the `student` account; numbers and home directory must be visible.
differs: If your user name is not `student`, use your own: `getent passwd $(whoami)`.
If the output is empty that account does not exist; check your name with `whoami`.

v05.title: Your identity
differs: On Ubuntu the sudo group is called `sudo`; on Rocky/Alma it is `wheel`.
If the UID is 0 you are running as root; switch to a normal user.

v06.title: Account list and shells
v06.text: List user name and shell side by side (first 8 lines).
differs: On Ubuntu the shell path may be `/usr/sbin/nologin`.
If `cut` fails, make sure you wrote the delimiter as `-d:` (no space).

q1.q: Which command shows failed login attempts?
q1.explain: `last` shows only successful logins; failed attempts are in `/var/log/btmp` and read with `lastb`.

q2.q: What does field 7 of a `/etc/passwd` line show?
q2.explain: Fields: name, x, UID, GID, comment, home, shell. Field 7 is the shell (e.g. /bin/bash or /sbin/nologin).

q3.q: In which file are password hashes stored?
q3.explain: Hashes are in /etc/shadow, readable only by root; the x in passwd indicates this.

options: It also finds LDAP/SSSD users besides the local file
It needs no permissions and shows passwords
q4.explain: getent queries all sources through NSS, so it returns users from the central directory too.

summary: `whoami`, `id` and `groups` show who you are and which groups you are in.
`/etc/passwd` has 7 fields (name, x, UID, GID, comment, home, shell); password hashes are in `/etc/shadow`.
`who` and `w` show current sessions, `last` successful and `lastb` failed past logins.
`getent` queries accounts without caring whether they come from a file or a central directory.

glossary.meaning: Numeric identity of a user and a group; root has UID 0.
A shell that blocks interactive login; used for service accounts.
Log files of successful and failed logins (`last` / `lastb`).
Average system load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
The layer that resolves account info from files or directory services, and the command to query it.
